newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel says favours electronic money.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel says favours electronic money.

text.p: Israel's central bank said on Tuesday it favoured the introduction of electronic money in the country, but added its role should be restricted to supervising such a system.
Electronic money includes a variety of computer-based payment schemes, such as smart cards which represent "virtual cash" and can be used to make various purchases.

The Bank of Israel said in a statement that its governor, Jacob Frenkel, had accepted the recommendations of an internal committee which found that electronic money could bring "great benefit" to the economy.
"But the committee does not deem it desirable for the Bank of Israel to be involved directly in issuing electronic money," the statement said.
"Such involvement could hurt the incentive of the private sector to develop on its own technological initiatives in this field," it said.

A task force set up in 1995 by the Group of 10 (G-10) central bankers has already examined "smart cards", which contain microchips that store cash value. It found the microchip cards more difficult to counterfeit than plastic cards with magnetic strips.
A G-10 report said electronic money could make economies more efficient by reducing cash handling costs and improving speed and convenience for consumers.
The Israeli committee said non-banking institutions should be allowed to issue electronic money "as long as they meet certain conditions that will be set by the governor of the Bank of Israel".

Legislation should be sought, the committee said, to give the Bank of Israel a central supervisory role in licensing organisations that will issue electronic money, protecting the consumer and setting rules on reporting and auditing.
